blocks.html: After studying this chapter, you will be able to:

items.html: explain project-based learning and why it matters
follow the steps of a software project, from choosing a problem to presenting the result
divide the work in a team and plan a timeline
write test cases, and tell apart black-box and white-box testing
prepare a project report in a standard format
read, run and extend a complete C++ project that uses classes, files, exceptions, sorting and searching
choose a project and know which chapters of this book it uses

blocks.html: In project-based learning, you learn by building something real that solves a problem, instead of only reading about it. A project brings together everything in this book: exceptions (Chapter 1), files (Chapter 2), data structures (Chapters 3–4), sorting and searching (Chapters 5–6), data analysis (Chapter 7), databases (Chapters 8–9), and networking and security ideas (Chapters 10–12).

items.html: You see how separate topics fit together in one working program.
You practise teamwork, planning and communication, the skills every software job needs.
You learn to find and fix bugs, which no textbook can fully teach.
A good project becomes part of your portfolio for college admissions, internships and jobs.
Identify the problem. Choose a real problem from your school, home or neighbourhood. Example: "Patients at a small clinic wait in long queues because appointments are written in a register."

Gather the requirements. Talk to the users (the receptionist, the doctor). List what the program must do (book, cancel, list by doctor) and the rules it must follow (no double booking; a mobile number must have 10 digits).
Plan. Divide the work among the team members and set a timeline (Section 13.3).
Design. Decide the data (structures, classes, files or tables), the menu, and the flow of each feature. Draw a flowchart or class diagram.
Code. Build one feature at a time. Compile and test often. Use meaningful names and comments.
Test. Run planned test cases, including wrong inputs (Section 13.4). Fix the bugs and test again.
Document. Write the project report (Section 13.5) and a short user guide.
Present and get feedback. Show the project to your class or the real users, and note their suggestions for the next version.

blocks.html: Testing means running the program with planned inputs to check that it behaves correctly, especially with wrong or unusual input.
A test case is one planned check: the input, the expected output, and the actual output observed.

blocks.html: Boundary values find many bugs: test just inside and just outside every limit, for example a mobile number of 9, 10 and 11 digits, or marks of −1, 0, 100 and 101.
A good report lets someone who has never seen your project understand, run and judge it.

items.html: Cover page: the project title, the names and roll numbers of the team, the class, the school and the year.
Certificate and acknowledgement, signed by the teacher.
Contents.
Introduction: the problem, who the users are, and why the project matters.
Requirements: what the system must do, and the hardware and software needed (for example a computer with g++ and C++17).
Design: the data structures, classes and files or tables, the menu, and the flowcharts.
Source code: well-commented and properly indented.
Output screens: screenshots of each feature, including the error messages.

lessons.title: 13.6 Complete sample project: Clinic Appointment Manager

blocks.html: This is the clinic project that has grown chapter by chapter in this book, now as one complete, working program. It has been compiled with g++ -std=c++17 -Wall -Wextra with no warnings, and tested with the test cases of Section 13.4.
Problem: a small clinic in Patna writes appointments in a register. Patients are sometimes double-booked, and the receptionist cannot quickly see a doctor's day.

blocks.html: time.

blocks.html: the right format.

items.html: Cancel an appointment by its ID.
Show all appointments in date and time order.
Show one doctor's appointments for one day, in time order.
Find all appointments for a mobile number.
Keep the data after the program is closed.
Never crash on wrong input.

rows: struct Appointment (id, patient, phone, doctor, date, time)
Text file appointments.csv , one line per appointment

blocks.caption: Figure 13.2 · design of the Clinic Appointment Manager

blocks.html: File format (appointments.csv ):
Dates are stored as YYYY-MM-DD so that sorting the text also sorts the dates correctly:
"2026-11-05" < "2026-12-01" . For the same reason, times are stored as HH:MM in 24-
hour form.
Compile and run: g++ -std=c++17 clinic.cpp -o clinic and then ./clinic (on Windows, clinic.exe ).

items.html: Project-based learning means learning by building a real solution. It joins all the topics of the book together.
Steps: identify the problem, gather requirements, plan, design, code, test, document, then present and improve. Steps 4–6 repeat in iterations.
Teams share roles (leader, designer, developers, tester and documenter), and everyone codes and can explain the code.

A test case lists the input, the expected output and the actual output. Test wrong and boundary inputs as well as normal ones. Black-box testing checks behaviour; white- box testing checks the code paths.
A project report covers the introduction, requirements, design, code, output, testing, limitations and bibliography.
The Clinic Appointment Manager shows classes, vectors, CSV file handling, user- defined exceptions, RAII, sorting with lambdas and searching together in one working program.
